Organocatalytic Asymmetric C(sp 2)/C0H Allylic
Alkylation: Enantioselective Synthesis of
Tetrasubstituted Allenoates
Yimin Hu, Wangyu Shi, Bing Zheng, Jianning Liao, Wei Wang, Yongjun Wu, and
Hongchao Guo*
Angewandte
ChemieCommunications
How to cite: Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2020, 59, 19820 – 19824
International Edition: doi.org/10.1002/anie.202009460
German Edition: doi.org/10.1002/ange.202009460

Asymmetric allylic alkylation is one of the most useful
carbon-carbon bond construction tools in synthesis of natural
products and biologically valuable molecules. [1] It displayed
the powerful ability to transform achiral, prochiral, or chiral
racemic material to enantiopure compounds. Asymmetric
allylic alkylation reactions such as Tsuji–T rost allylation
reactions via p-allyl species,
[2] and organocatalytic allylic
alkylation of modified Morita-Baylis–Hillman (MBH)
adducts[3] have thus intensely been studied. In general, in
Tsuji–T rost allylation reactions and organocatalytic allylic
alkylations, active methylene compounds having one or two
electron-withdrawing groups, enamines and enolates act as
the soft carbon nucleophiles (Scheme 1 a and b). Asymmetric
process occurs at highly activated sp
3 center of these soft
carbon nucleophiles, on which the proton has certain acidity,
leading to asymmetric allylation of activated C(sp 3)-H func-
tional group (Scheme 1 a and b). To the best of our knowl-
edge, asymmetric C(sp
2)-H allylation has not been reported in
Tsuji–T rost allylation reactions and organocatalytic allylic
alkylations. This triggered our keen interest, and inspired us
to investigate application of the electron-deficeint allenes in
these asymmetric allylation reactions, which may provide
a new approach to synthesize chiral allenes.
Axially chiral allenes are a key structural moiety in many
natural products, bioactive molecules and chiral catalysts.
[4]
New catalytic asymmetric reactions for their synthesis,
especially for synthesis of chiral molecules with multiple
elements of chirality by simultaneously controlling two
different elements of stereogenicity,
[5] are highly desirable.
While metal-catalyzed asymmetric reactions showed great
ability in synthesis of chiral allenes,
[6] organocatalytic asym-
metric tools also demonstrated their practicability, but these
organocatalytic methods still remain limited.
[7, 8] Most organo-
catalytic processes handled synthesis of di- or trisubstituted
allenes,[7a–g] and those synthetic accesses to chiral tetrasub-
stituted allenes are rare. [7h–n, 8] Among various approaches for
chiral allenes, enantioselective functionalization of racemic
allenes is an attractive and challenging one. Generally, a-
hydrogen of allenoates and allene ketones has relatively low
pK
a and displays certain acidity. In principle, it can be
deprotonated and acts as a nucleophile. In 2013, Maruoka and
co-workers reported alleno-Mannich and alkylation reactions
of allenoates under phase-transfer catalysis.
[8] In both reac-
tions, the facile generation of cumulenolate under phase-
transfer conditions was a key step. This pioneering work
provided an concise method for synthesis of chiral tetrasub-
stituted allenes. With the use of allene anion as a nucleophile,
we herein report an unprecedented organocatalytic C(sp
2)-H
allylation of racemic trisubstituted allenoates with MBH
carbonates to access axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenoates
with good to excellent diastereo- and enantioselectivities
(Scheme 1 c).
At the beginning of our study, the reaction of trisubsti-
tuted allenoate 1a and MBH carbonate 2a in CH
2Cl2 was
used as a model reaction to find the best catalyst (Table 1).
The tertiary amine catalyst DABCO (1,4-diazabicyclo-
[2.2.2]octane) showed excellent performance, and the product
was obtained in 95 % yield in 0.3 h, although the diastereo-
selectivity was poor (entry 1). After getting these results, we
next carefully evaluated the performance of various chiral
Lewis bases, including cinchona-derived tertiary amines
(LB1–LB6) and phosphines ( LB7–LB8) with different scaf-
folds and functional groups. Quinine ( LB1) only led to trace
of product (entry 2). Other cinchona-derived tertiary amines
LB2–LB6 showed good catalytic activity, but both diaster-
eoselectvity and enantioselectivity were not satisfactory
(entries 3–7). Disappointingly, chiral phosphines ( LB7–LB8)
did not catalyze this reaction (entries 8–9). Compared with
other catalysts, b-isocinchonine ( LB4) was identified as the
most effective catalyst in terms of catalytic activity and
stereoselectivity, giving the product 3a a in 89 % yield with
Abstract: Herein we describe the first organocatalytic asym-
metric C(sp
2)/C0H allylation of racemic trisubstituted allenoates
with Morita–Baylis–Hillman (MBH) carbonates to access
axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenoates. Various trisubstituted
allenoates and MBH carbonates were well tolerated under mild
reaction conditions, providing novel chiral tetrasubstituted
allenoates with adjacent axial chirality and tertiary carbon
stereocenters in high yields with good to excellent diastereo-
selectivities and enantioselectivities.

70 % ee, albeit with poor diastereoselectivity (entry 5).
Solvent screening (entries 10–15) revealed that diethyl ether
was the optimal solvent, which resulted in 91 % yield with
84 % ee and > 20:1 dr (entry 12). Using ethyl ether as the
solvent, lowering the temperature helped slightly increasing
ee value from 84 % to 88 % (entry 16). The addition of 3 /C138 MS
also favored enantioselectivity (entry 17). All these results
indicated that the optimal reaction conditions were: using
20 mol % of LB4 in diethyl ether at /C020
8C with 3 /C138 MS as an
additive.
With the optimal reaction conditions in hand, we explored
the substrate scope of trisubstituted allenoates 1 (Table 2).
The asymmetric allylation reaction produced the tetrasubsti-
tuted allenoates in 78–99 % yields with 17:1 to > 20:1 dr and
90–92 % ee (entries 1–14). The electronic and steric properties
of substituents on the phenyl groups of the allenoates had
little effect on the reactivities and stereoselectivities
(entries 1–14). In particular, the substrates with highly
electron-deficient substituents on the benzene ring of the
allenoates, including 4-NO
2C6H4, 4-CNC 6H4 and 4-CF 3C6H4
substituted ones, afforded the corresponding products in 89–
91 % yields with 90–91 % ee (entries 12–14). We next inves-
tigated the impact of the R
2 groups linked to ketone carbonyl
on the reaction. Both alkyl groups such as ethyl, phenethyl
and phenyl group in the allenoates had no remarkable impact
on the reactivities and stereoselectivities, and all these
allenoates performed well to give the tetrasubstituted alle-
noates in 75–90 % yield with > 20:1 dr and 90–92 % ee
(entries 15–17). When the R
1 group was an alkyl group,
excellent diastereoselectivity and enantioselectivity were
maintained, although the yield dropped (entry 18).
We next examined the reaction of trisubstituted allenoates
1a with a variety of MBH carbonates 2 (Table 3). Diverse
aryl-substituted MBH carbonates were compatible with the
optimal conditions, and the reactions displayed high yields,
excellent enantioselectivities and diastereoselectivities in
most cases (entries 1–20). It appears that the position of the
substituents on the phenyl ring of the R group did not
significantly affect the reaction. The disubstituted substrates
also worked to give the product 3a h in 99 % yield with > 20:1
dr and 90 % ee (entry 7). The substrates with 1-naphthyl and
2-naphthyl groups adapted well to the optimal reaction
conditions and provided the corresponding products 3a t and

3a u in 99 %yield/90 %ee and 89 %yield/94 %ee, respectively
(entries 19–20). The absolute configuration of the products
was unambiguously assigned through X-ray crystallographic
analysis of the product 3a e.
[9]
As indicated in Scheme 2, the allylation reaction on the
large scale proceeded smoothly to produce the product 3a a in
82 % yield with > 20:1 dr and 90 % ee. The tetrasubstituted
allenoate products have several functional groups such as
carbonyl, ester and carbon-carbon double bond, which
provide a nice chance for further elaboration. T reatment of
chiral allene 3a a with nitrilimine 4 in the presence of Et
3N
gave the pyrazoline derivative 5 in 72 % yield with > 20:1 dr
and 90 % ee. The cycloaddition of the chiral allene 3a a with
nitrile oxides 6 led to a dihydroisoxazole derivative 7 in 94 %
yield with > 20:1 dr and 90 % ee.[9]
As indicated in Scheme 3, a plausible mechanism for this
asymmetric allylation was proposed. The addition of the
catalyst LB4 to MBH carbonate 2a gave the intermediate A
with simultaneous generation of tert-butoxy carbanion, which
deprotonated trisubstituted allenoate 1a to afford the allene
carbanion B. Subsequent conjugate addition of the nucleo-
phile B to the intermediate A led to formation of the
tetrasubstituted allenoate intermediate C, which then pro-
duced the final product 3a a through regeneration of the
tertiary amine catalyst. In the transition state TS, due to bulky
steric hindrance of the catalyst, the allene carbanion B attacks
the Re face of the olefinic bond in the intermediate A, which
determines the absolute configuration of the product.
In summary, we have developed the first organocatalytic
asymmetric C(sp 2)-H allylation of trisubstituted allenoates
with MBH carbonates to access tetrasubstituted allenoates.
V arious trisubstituted allenoates and MBH carbonates were
well tolerated under mild reaction conditions, providing novel
tetrasubstituted allenoates with adjacent axial chirality and
tertiary carbon stereocenters in high yields with good to
excellent enantioselectivities and diastereoselectivities.
